parsing_res_list.block_content: The flexural stiffness of a reinforced masonry component should be based on the average of the cracked moment of inertia and the net, uncracked moment of inertia using Equation 6-10. This is an approximate approach that is not based on measurements of the actual cracking that occurs during dynamic blast response, but is consistent with the approach recommended for reinforced concrete in Section 4-15.This approach has been assumed in previous comparisons where the dynamic deflections calculated in SDOF analyses using Equation 6-10 compared well, on the average, to measured values (Oswald et al, 2006). The importance of the moment of inertia is often reduced by the fact that most wall deflection typically occurs after yielding of the flexural reinforcing steel, when the wall stifness is assumed equal to zero in the SDOF analysis methodology, so that most of the dynamic deflection is not affected by the moment of inertia. The cracked moment of inertia can be calculated using a simplified approach in Equation 6-11, or it can be calculated with the methodology for reinforced concrete in Section 4-15 using $E_{m}$ from Equation 6-2 in place of the modulus of elasticity for concrete (Ec). For solid masonry units, the value of $I_{n}$ is equal to the moment of inertia of the gross section. Values of $I_{n}$ for ungrouted or partially grouted CMU can be determined using information in Section 6-7.2.1.

$I_{a}=$ the average moment of inertia for the net section and cracked section $(i n^{4}/i n)$ 
$I_{n}=$ the moment of inertia of the net masonry section (in4/in) (see Equation 6-1)
$I_{\tt C}=$ the moment of inertia of the cracked masonry section (in/in) (see Equation 6-11)
$d=$ effective depth (distance from the extreme compression fiber to the centroid of the tension reinforcement)

Unreinforced masonry walls may not be used for new construction. The adequacy of existing unreinforced masonry walls may be evaluated in accordance with Section 6-7.Accordingly, these walls may not be placed in tension and must satisfy the shear (diagonal tension) and direct shear requirements of Sections 6-7.3.4 and 6-7.3.5,

Moment of Inertia.
The flexural stiffness of a reinforced masonry component should be based on the
average of the cracked moment of inertia and the net, uncracked moment of inertia
using Equation 6-10. This is an approximate approach that is not based on
measurements of the actual cracking that occurs during dynamic blast response, but is
consistent with the approach recommended for reinforced concrete in Section 4-15.
This approach has been assumed in previous comparisons where the dynamic
deflections calculated in SDOF analyses using Equation 6-10 compared well, on the
average, to measured values (Oswald et al, 2006). The importance of the moment of
inertia is often reduced by the fact that most wall deflection typically occurs after yielding
of the flexural reinforcing steel, when the wall stifness is assumed equal to zero in the
SDOF analysis methodology, so that most of the dynamic deflection is not affected by
the moment of inertia. The cracked moment of inertia can be calculated using a
simplified approach in Equation 6-11, or it can be calculated with the methodology for
